title: Efficiency — getting more out of what you put in
examTip: Efficiency has no units. It is a ratio between 0 and 1 (or 0–100%). Always check whether the question wants a decimal or a percentage.
introTips: Most devices waste some energy as heat or sound.
A higher efficiency number means less energy is wasted.
You can work out efficiency using energy (joules) or power (watts). It is the same formula and the same answer.
intro: Imagine a petrol car engine gets 100 units of energy from fuel. Only 25 units end up as useful motion. Efficiency tells you how good a device is at turning input energy into something useful. It matters because wasted energy costs money. It also uses up resources faster and adds to climate change. Efficiency is why LED bulbs replaced filament bulbs.

keyPoints.heading: What efficiency means
keyPoints.content: Efficiency is the proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred. Most devices waste some energy, usually as thermal energy (heat) or sound. An electric heater is close to 100% efficient. This is because heating is its useful output. The equation is: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. You can also give it as a percentage: efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%. Efficiency has no units. It is a pure ratio (or percentage). The highest possible efficiency is 1.0 (or 100%). That would be a machine that wastes nothing. A machine with efficiency 0.75 transfers 75% of its input energy usefully. It wastes 25% to heat, sound or other stores we don't want.
writeBullets: Efficiency — the fraction of input energy that is usefully transferred. No units, between 0 and 1
Useful output energy — energy transferred to the store we want
Total input energy — all the energy supplied to the device, including what is wasted
Efficiency as a decimal — useful output ÷ total input (for example, 0.75)
Efficiency as a percentage — (useful output ÷ total input) × 100% (for example, 75%)

keyTerms.def: The proportion of input energy that is usefully transferred; efficiency = useful output ÷ total input
Energy transferred to the intended output store — the energy that does the job we want
All energy supplied to a device, including both useful and wasted portions

keyPoints.memTip: Efficiency = useful ÷ total. Think 'useful over all'.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to mix up useful output and total input. The total input is always the bigger number.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating efficiency
keyPoints.content: The efficiency equation works with both energy (in joules) and power (in watts): - efficiency = useful output energy (J) ÷ total input energy (J) - efficiency = useful power output (W) ÷ total power input (W) Worked example 1: a motor gets 500 J of electrical energy. It does 375 J of useful work → efficiency = 375 ÷ 500 = 0.75 (75%). Worked example 2: a lamp has a total power input of 10 W. Its useful power output is 9 W → efficiency = 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9 (90%). Worked example 3: a petrol car engine has an input power of 100 kW. It has a useful power output of 25 kW → efficiency = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 (25%). The other 75 kW is wasted as thermal energy and sound. You can also rearrange it: - useful output = efficiency × total input - total input = useful output ÷ efficiency
writeBullets: Efficiency = useful output energy (J) ÷ total input energy (J). Works with joules
Efficiency = useful power output (W) ÷ total power input (W). Works with watts too
Rearrangement: useful output = efficiency × total input
Rearrangement: total input = useful output ÷ efficiency
Converting to %: multiply the decimal efficiency by 100

keyTerms.def: efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (or useful power ÷ total input power)
Total input energy minus useful output energy — always positive in a real device

keyPoints.memTip: Worked examples: motor 375/500=0.75; lamp 9/10=0.9; car engine 25/100=0.25. Practise these numbers.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Always write out the formula first. Then substitute, then calculate. This picks up method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

keyPoints.heading: Comparing efficiencies of different devices
keyPoints.content: You may be asked to compare devices. The question gives you the values you need. Work out the efficiency of each device, then compare them. The device with the higher efficiency wastes less of its input energy. - LED bulbs are more efficient than Incandescent (filament) bulbs. For the same input power, an LED bulb gives out more useful light. - Electric motors are usually more efficient than Petrol car engines. Most of the energy from the fuel is wasted as heat in the engine and exhaust. Worked example: motor A has a total power input of 200 W and a useful power output of 150 W. Motor B has a total power input of 500 W and a useful power output of 300 W. A = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75. B = 300 ÷ 500 = 0.60. So motor A is more efficient.
writeBullets: Compare devices using the values given in the question
Work out the efficiency of each device first, then compare
Higher efficiency — less of the input energy is wasted
LED bulb — more efficient than a filament bulb. More of its input energy is transferred as light
Incandescent bulb — wastes most of its input energy by heating the surroundings
Petrol engine — most energy from the fuel is wasted as thermal energy and sound

keyTerms.def: Old-style filament light bulb — wastes most of its input energy by heating
Light Emitting Diode — more efficient than a filament bulb at transferring energy usefully as light

keyPoints.memTip: Compare with the numbers you are given. Higher efficiency = less energy wasted.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Comparing devices is a common exam question. Use the values given in the question. Work out each efficiency, then compare.

keyPoints.heading: Improving efficiency
keyPoints.content: We can improve efficiency in several ways: - Reducing friction: oil between moving parts → less kinetic energy wasted as thermal energy. - Better insulation: less thermal energy lost from hot surfaces to the surroundings. Insulating a boiler is one example. - More efficient components: LEDs instead of filament bulbs, and electric motors instead of petrol engines. A more efficient device needs less input energy for the same useful output.
writeBullets: Lubrication — reduces friction between moving parts, cutting wasted thermal energy
Insulation — slows thermal energy loss from hot surfaces to the surroundings
Efficient components — LEDs and electric motors use less energy for the same output

keyTerms.def: Using oil between moving parts to reduce friction, so less energy is wasted by heating

keyPoints.memTip: To improve efficiency, cut the wasted energy: reduce friction, insulate, use better parts.
keyPoints.tutor_note: When asked how to improve efficiency, name the method. Then say which wasted energy transfer it reduces.

tables.title: Useful and wasted energy in common devices

0.question: A device receives 800 J of energy and usefully transfers 560 J. What is its efficiency?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! efficiency = 560 ÷ 800 = 0.70 = 70%. The other 30% (240 J) is wasted.
0.wrongFeedback: Use efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 560 ÷ 800 = 0.70. Multiply by 100 for a percentage: 70%.

1.question: A motor has a total power input of 400 W. Its useful power output is 300 W. What is its efficiency?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input = 300 ÷ 400 = 0.75 = 75%.
1.wrongFeedback: Use efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input = 300 ÷ 400 = 0.75. Efficiency has no units, and it is never more than 1.

2.question: Lamp A has a total power input of 40 W and gives out 8 W of light. Lamp B has a total power input of 10 W and gives out 4 W of light. Which lamp is more efficient?
options: Lamp B, because its efficiency is 0.4 and lamp A's is 0.2
Lamp A, because it gives out more light
Lamp A, because it uses more power
2.correctFeedback: Correct! Lamp A: 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2. Lamp B: 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4. Lamp B transfers a bigger fraction of its input usefully.
2.wrongFeedback: Work out each efficiency first. Lamp A: 8 ÷ 40 = 0.2. Lamp B: 4 ÷ 10 = 0.4. The higher efficiency wins, so lamp B is more efficient.

3.question: Oil is put between the moving parts of a machine. Why does this make the machine more efficient?
options: It reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating
It adds energy to the machine's chemical store
It increases the total input energy
It stops all energy being dissipated
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Lubrication reduces friction. Less energy is wasted as thermal energy, so more of the input is transferred usefully.
3.wrongFeedback: Oil is a lubricant. It reduces friction between moving parts. So less energy is wasted by heating, and the efficiency goes up.

commonMistakes: Putting total input on top instead of useful output. Always put USEFUL output on top: efficiency = useful output ÷ total input.
Thinking efficiency can be more than 1 (or 100%). That would break the conservation of energy. Always check your answer is ≤ 1.
Forgetting to convert between decimal and percentage. If a question asks for a percentage, multiply by 100.
Mixing up power efficiency and energy efficiency. They give the same result. Keep the units the same: both in W, or both in J.
Saying a device 'creates' or 'destroys' energy. It transfers energy. The total input always equals useful output + wasted energy.
examTips: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input. Check: is the answer between 0 and 1? If not, you have divided the wrong way round.
You may be given power values instead of energy values. The same formula works: efficiency = useful power output ÷ total power input.
When comparing devices, work out each efficiency from the values given. Explain what 'more efficient' means for energy transfer. Don't just say 'wastes less'.
revisionCardBullets: Efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer (no units)
Maximum efficiency = 1.0 (100%). Most real devices are less than this
Also works with power: efficiency = useful power output (W) ÷ total power input (W)
An electric heater is close to 100% efficient, because heating is its useful output
An LED bulb is more efficient than a filament bulb
Compare devices by working out each efficiency from the values given
Improve efficiency: lubrication, insulation, efficient components
Wasted energy = total input − useful output (always positive)
